## Paper and figure

Delavaux, C. S., Crowther, T. W., Bever, J. D., Weigelt, P., & Gora, E. M. (2024). Mutualisms weaken the latitudinal diversity gradient among oceanic islands. *Nature*, **627**, 335–339. <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07110-y>.

I reconstruct **Figure 4** ([original figure](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07110-y/figures/4)). Its six panels compare pollination, mycorrhizal association, and nitrogen fixation. The upper panels show mainland species richness; the lower panels show each group's contribution to the island species deficit. Points show observations, lines show model predictions, and shaded bands show standard errors.

The figure meets four criteria: **facets**, **multiple layers**, **group mapped to color**, and **computed quantities** (fitted values and uncertainty bands). I preserve the six-panel structure using simple simulated data and quadratic regression.

## Part 1: Infer the data

### Variables and structure

Species richness counts species in a mainland flora. A group's contribution to the island deficit is its missing species divided by the total missing species; this differs from the fraction of that group's own species that is missing.

| Variable | Type | Values in my simulation |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | Identifier | 90 synthetic comparison locations |
| `latitude` | Continuous | Absolute latitude, uniform from 0 to 70 degrees |
| `type` | Categorical | Pollination, Mycorrhiza, N-fixation |
| `group` | Categorical | Biotic/Abiotic; AM/EM/NM; N-fixing/Non-N-fixing |
| `metric` | Categorical | Species richness or deficit contribution |
| `value` | Numeric | Positive integer species counts, or a dimensionless proportion from 0 to 1 |

AM and EM denote arbuscular and ectomycorrhizal association; NM denotes non-mycorrhizal plants. Each synthetic location contributes both metrics for every group, giving 1,260 plotted observations. These counts are simulation choices, not the paper's sample sizes.

### Generative description

Draw 90 latitudes uniformly between 0 and 70 degrees. For each group, let mean richness be `a + b * latitude + c * latitude^2`. Add independent normal noise with standard deviation equal to one quarter of this mean, round to an integer, and replace values below one with one. Counts will generally range from a few species to several thousand.

For deficit contributions, start with `p0 + p1 * latitude`, add uniform noise between −0.06 and 0.06, and replace weights below 0.005 with 0.005. Within each location and mutualism type, divide each weight by their sum, so the group contributions sum to one. The parameters are:

| Type | Group | a | b | c | p0 | p1 |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Pollination | Biotic | 6000 | −55 | −0.20 | 0.96 | −0.0055 |
| Pollination | Abiotic | 300 | 10 | −0.08 | 0.04 | 0.0055 |
| Mycorrhiza | AM | 5000 | −45 | −0.15 | 0.86 | −0.0040 |
| Mycorrhiza | EM | 150 | 15 | −0.13 | 0.02 | 0.0012 |
| Mycorrhiza | NM | 600 | 6 | −0.03 | 0.12 | 0.0028 |
| N-fixation | N-fixing | 600 | −8 | 0.025 | 0.74 | −0.0080 |
| N-fixation | Non-N-fixing | 5000 | 100 | −2.00 | 0.26 | 0.0080 |

These settings make biotically pollinated and AM plants dominate at low latitudes, with their contributions decreasing at higher latitudes. The N-fixing contribution also declines and eventually falls below the non-N-fixing contribution.

### Simplifications

I reuse the same synthetic latitude design for both metrics rather than modelling separate mainland and island samples. Contributions are generated directly, without reconstructing island inventories. Noise is independent across metrics and mutualism types; spatial correlation and environmental covariates are omitted. All parameters are chosen to resemble broad patterns. Quadratic regressions replace the original models. For convenience, I use the confidence bands supplied by `geom_smooth()` instead of reproducing the original one-standard-error bands; these bands describe uncertainty in the fitted mean, not individual observations.

## Part 2: Rebuild the figure

### Simulate the data

The code uses basic arithmetic and normal and uniform random numbers. It requires `ggplot2` and `colorspace`, in addition to Quarto's R dependencies; no external data are needed.

```{r}
#| label: simulate
seed <- 5014L
set.seed(seed)
library(ggplot2)
n <- 90L
confidence <- 0.95
parameters <- data.frame(
  type = c(rep("Pollination", 2), rep("Mycorrhiza", 3), rep("N-fixation", 2)),
  group = c("Biotic", "Abiotic", "AM", "EM", "NM", "N-fixing", "Non-N-fixing"),
  a = c(6000, 300, 5000, 150, 600, 600, 5000),
  b = c(-55, 10, -45, 15, 6, -8, 100),
  c = c(-0.20, -0.08, -0.15, -0.13, -0.03, 0.025, -2),
  p0 = c(0.96, 0.04, 0.86, 0.02, 0.12, 0.74, 0.26),
  p1 = c(-0.0055, 0.0055, -0.004, 0.0012, 0.0028, -0.008, 0.008)
)
locations <- data.frame(id = seq_len(n), latitude = runif(n, 0, 70))
d <- merge(locations, parameters, by = NULL)
mu <- with(d, a + b * latitude + c * latitude^2)
d$richness <- pmax(1, round(rnorm(nrow(d), mu, 0.25 * mu)))
weight <- with(d, p0 + p1 * latitude) + runif(nrow(d), -0.06, 0.06)
weight <- pmax(0.005, weight)
d$contribution <- weight / ave(weight, d$id, d$type, FUN = sum)
metrics <- c("Species richness (species)", "Deficit contribution (proportion)")
dat <- rbind(transform(d, metric = metrics[1], value = richness),
             transform(d, metric = metrics[2], value = contribution))
dat$type <- factor(dat$type, levels = unique(parameters$type))
dat$metric <- factor(dat$metric, levels = metrics)
dat$group <- factor(dat$group, levels = parameters$group)
```

### Reconstructed figure

Each curve is a simple quadratic regression: an intercept, latitude, and squared latitude. `geom_smooth()` fits the curves and draws their confidence bands automatically. Faceting repeats the same points, lines, and ribbons across all panels. The row labels state the response units.

```{r}
#| label: fig-reconstruction
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 7
palette <- c(Biotic = "#0072B2", Abiotic = "#D55E00", AM = "#0072B2",
             EM = "#D55E00", NM = "#666666", "N-fixing" = "#0072B2",
             "Non-N-fixing" = "#D55E00")
p <- ggplot(dat, aes(latitude, value, color = group)) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = group), alpha = 0.28, size = 1.1, stroke = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(aes(fill = group, linetype = group), method = "lm",
              formula = y ~ x + I(x^2), level = confidence,
              linewidth = 0.85, alpha = 0.18) +
  facet_grid(metric ~ type, scales = "free_y", switch = "y") +
  scale_color_manual(values = palette) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = palette, guide = "none") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 17, 16, 17, 15, 16, 17)) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "dashed", "solid", "dashed",
                                  "dotdash", "solid", "dashed")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 70, 20), expand = expansion(mult = 0.03)) +
  labs(x = "Absolute latitude (degrees)", y = NULL,
       color = "Plant group", shape = "Plant group", linetype = "Plant group") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), legend.position = "bottom",
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"), strip.placement = "outside",
        panel.spacing = grid::unit(1.1, "lines")) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 1, override.aes = list(alpha = 1, fill = NA)))
p
```

::: {.figure-caption}
**Figure.** Simulated reconstruction of the selected published figure, with `r n` comparison locations, `r nrow(parameters)` groups nested within `r nlevels(dat$type)` mutualism types, and `r nrow(dat)` observations across `r nlevels(dat$metric) * nlevels(dat$type)` panels. Points are simulated observations; lines are quadratic regression fits; ribbons are `r 100 * confidence`% confidence intervals for the fitted mean (the original uses standard-error bands). Seed: `r seed`. Both metrics share a synthetic latitude design; these are not the paper's observations.
:::

### Colorblindness check

Blue and vermilion distinguish each two-group comparison, with gray added for the third mycorrhizal group. Colors repeat only across separate mutualism columns. Shapes and line patterns provide additional cues. The following swatches simulate three types of color vision deficiency at full severity.

```{r}
#| label: fig-palette-check
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 2.1
colors <- c("#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#666666")
vision <- list(Original = identity, Protanopia = colorspace::protan,
               Deuteranopia = colorspace::deutan, Tritanopia = colorspace::tritan)
op <- par(mar = c(1, 9, 1, 1))
plot.new()
plot.window(xlim = c(0, 3), ylim = c(0, 4))
for (i in seq_along(vision)) {
  rect(0:2, 4 - i, 1:3, 4.8 - i, col = vision[[i]](colors), border = NA)
  text(0, 4.4 - i, names(vision)[i], pos = 2, xpd = NA)
}
par(op)
```

## One improvement to the original

The original figure could add distinct point shapes and line patterns so its groups remain identifiable without color.
